requirements.original: Lowest Binary **xor**
requirements.canonical: The binary `xor` operator IS of higher precedence than the binary `or` operator.

ambiguity.issue: The PDF rendering places the label 'Lowest' at the `xor` row although `or` is listed after it; the label most likely spans the last rows, so `or` is taken as the lowest-precedence operator.
readings: The binary `xor` operator IS of higher precedence than the binary `or` operator, and `or` IS of the lowest precedence.
The binary `xor` operator IS of the lowest precedence, and `or` IS of equal or higher precedence.

requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.0 -- Lowest Binary **xor**

requirements.original: Binary **or**
requirements.canonical: The binary `or` operator IS of the lowest precedence of all operators.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.0 -- Binary **or**

requirements.original: NOTE: Dot notation ("."), index notation (" [ ] ") and the decoding notation (" => ") should be evaluated from left to right, just after the evaluation of the parentheses (" ( ) ") operator and before the evaluation of the ispresent, ischosen, isvalue, isbound operators.
requirements.canonical: Dot notation, index notation and decoding notation (`=>`) SHOULD be evaluated from left to right, just after the parentheses operator and before the `ispresent`, `ischosen`, `isvalue` and `isbound` operators.

ambiguity.issue: The evaluation order is given in a NOTE with 'should', but the following normative sentence (7.1.0-s056) states it as an equivalence; it is unclear whether it is a recommendation or a binding rule. The NOTE is kept as recommendation; the binding rule is recorded as 7.1.0-056a.
readings: Dot notation, index notation and decoding notation SHOULD be evaluated from left to right, after parentheses and before the presence checking operators (recommendation).
Dot notation, index notation and decoding notation SHALL be evaluated from left to right, after parentheses and before the presence checking operators (binding rule).

requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.0 -- NOTE: Dot notation ("."), index notation (" [ ] ") and the decoding notation (" => ") should be evaluated from left to right, just after the evaluation of the parentheses (" ( ) ") operator and before the evaluation of the ispresent, ischosen, isvalue, isbound operators.

requirements.original: That is: a.b[x].d=>e.f is equivalent to `((((a.b)[x]).d)=>e).f`
requirements.canonical: The expression `a.b[x].d=>e.f` IS equivalent to `((((a.b)[x]).d)=>e).f`, i.e. dot, index and decoding notations are evaluated left to right.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.0 -- That is: a.b[x].d=>e.f is equivalent to `((((a.b)[x]).d)=>e).f`

requirements.original: Operands of these operators shall be of integer values (including derivations of integer) or floating-point numbers (including derivations of float, containing numeric values only), except for mod and rem which shall be used with integer (including derivations of integer) types only.
requirements.canonical: An operand of an arithmetic operator SHALL be an integer value (including values of types derived from integer) or a float value (including values of types derived from float) containing a numeric value only.

ambiguity.issue: 'containing numeric values only' could exclude the special float values infinity, -infinity and not_a_number, which contradicts 7.1.1-s003; it is also not stated whether integer and float operands may be mixed. Reading 1 (special values allowed per IEEE 754, no mixing) is chosen.
readings: An operand of an arithmetic operator SHALL be an integer or float value, the special float values being allowed with IEEE 754 semantics, and both operands SHALL be of the same root type.
An operand of an arithmetic operator SHALL be an integer value or a float value that is not infinity, -infinity or not_a_number.
An arithmetic operator MAY combine an integer operand with a float operand.

requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- Operands of these operators shall be of integer values (including derivations of integer) or floating-point numbers (including derivations of float, containing numeric values only), except for mod and rem which shall be used with integer (including derivations of integer) types only.

requirements.original: Operands of these operators shall be of integer values (including derivations of integer) or floating-point numbers (including derivations of float, containing numeric values only), except for mod and rem which shall be used with integer (including derivations of integer) types only.
requirements.canonical: An operand of the `mod` or `rem` operator SHALL be of type integer or of a type derived from integer.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- Operands of these operators shall be of integer values (including derivations of integer) or floating-point numbers (including derivations of float, containing numeric values only), except for mod and rem which shall be used with integer (including derivations of integer) types only.

requirements.original: The usage of the special float values infinity, -infinity and not_a_number in arithmetic operators shall follow the rules defined in IEEE 754 [6].
requirements.canonical: The use of the special float values `infinity`, `-infinity` and `not_a_number` in arithmetic operators SHALL follow the rules defined in IEEE 754.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- The usage of the special float values infinity, -infinity and not_a_number in arithmetic operators shall follow the rules defined in IEEE 754 [6].

requirements.original: With integer types, the result type of arithmetic operations is integer.
requirements.canonical: The result type of an arithmetic operation on integer operands IS integer.
requirements.condition: the operands are of integer type
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- With integer types, the result type of arithmetic operations is integer.

requirements.original: With float types, the result type of arithmetic operations is float.
requirements.canonical: The result type of an arithmetic operation on float operands IS float.
requirements.condition: the operands are of float type
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- With float types, the result type of arithmetic operations is float.

requirements.original: In the case where plus (+) or minus (-) is used as the unary operator the rules for operands apply as well.
requirements.canonical: The operand of the unary `+` or unary `-` operator SHALL obey the same operand rules as the binary arithmetic operators (integer or numeric float value).
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- In the case where plus (+) or minus (-) is used as the unary operator the rules for operands apply as well.

requirements.original: The result of using the minus operator is the negative value of the operand if it was positive and vice versa.
requirements.canonical: The result of the unary `-` operator IS the negated value of the operand (negative for a positive operand and positive for a negative operand).
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- The result of using the minus operator is the negative value of the operand if it was positive and vice versa.

requirements.original: The result of using the plus operator is the value of the operand, i.e. a positive value if the operand value was positive and a negative value if the operand value was negative.
requirements.canonical: The result of the unary `+` operator IS the value of the operand unchanged.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- The result of using the plus operator is the value of the operand, i.e. a positive value if the operand value was positive and a negative value if the operand value was negative.

requirements.original: a) `integer values gives the whole integer part of the value resulting from dividing the first integer by` the second (i.e. fractions are discarded);
requirements.canonical: The result of the division operator `/` on two integer values IS the whole integer part of the quotient of the first integer by the second, with the fraction discarded.

ambiguity.issue: 'Whole integer part' does not state the rounding direction for negative quotients; truncation toward zero is chosen because it is consistent with the rem definition and table 7.
readings: Integer division truncates the quotient toward zero (e.g. -7/2 = -3).
Integer division rounds the quotient toward negative infinity (e.g. -7/2 = -4).

requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- a) `integer values gives the whole integer part of the value resulting from dividing the first integer by` the second (i.e. fractions are discarded);

requirements.original: b) numeric float values gives the float value resulting from dividing the first float by the second (i.e. fractions are not discarded).
requirements.canonical: The result of the division operator `/` on two numeric float values IS the float quotient of the first float by the second, without discarding fractions.
requirements.condition: both operands are numeric float values
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- b) numeric float values gives the float value resulting from dividing the first float by the second (i.e. fractions are not discarded).

requirements.original: The operators rem and mod compute on operands of type integer and have a result of type integer.
requirements.canonical: The result type of the `rem` and `mod` operators IS integer.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- The operators rem and mod compute on operands of type integer and have a result of type integer.

requirements.original: The operations x rem y and x mod y compute the rest that remains from an integer division of x by y.
requirements.canonical: The result of `x rem y` and of `x mod y` IS the remainder of the integer division of x by y.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- The operations x rem y and x mod y compute the rest that remains from an integer division of x by y.

requirements.original: Therefore, they are only defined for non-zero operands y.
requirements.canonical: The right operand y of the `rem` or `mod` operator SHALL NOT be zero.

ambiguity.issue: 'only defined for non-zero operands y' does not say whether a zero divisor is a compile-time error (for constants) or a runtime error, or whether the result is just undefined.
readings: A zero right operand of `rem` or `mod` SHALL cause an error (at compile time if known statically, otherwise at runtime).
The result of `rem` or `mod` with a zero right operand IS undefined and no error is required.

requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- Therefore, they are only defined for non-zero operands y.

requirements.original: For positive x and y, both x `rem` `y and x` `mod` `y have the same result but for` negative arguments they differ.
requirements.canonical: For positive x and y, `x rem y` IS equal to `x mod y`; for negative arguments the results differ.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- For positive x and y, both x `rem` `y and x` `mod` `y have the same result but for` negative arguments they differ.

requirements.original: x rem y = x - y * (x/y) x mod y = x rem |y| when x >= 0 = 0 when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0 = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0
requirements.canonical: `x rem y` IS defined as `x - y * (x/y)`.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- x rem y = x - y * (x/y) x mod y = x rem |y| when x >= 0 = 0 when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0 = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0

requirements.original: x rem y = x - y * (x/y) x mod y = x rem |y| when x >= 0 = 0 when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0 = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0
requirements.canonical: When x >= 0, `x mod y` IS equal to `x rem |y|`.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- x rem y = x - y * (x/y) x mod y = x rem |y| when x >= 0 = 0 when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0 = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0

requirements.original: x rem y = x - y * (x/y) x mod y = x rem |y| when x >= 0 = 0 when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0 = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0
requirements.canonical: When x < 0 and `x rem |y|` = 0, `x mod y` IS 0.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- x rem y = x - y * (x/y) x mod y = x rem |y| when x >= 0 = 0 when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0 = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0

requirements.original: x rem y = x - y * (x/y) x mod y = x rem |y| when x >= 0 = 0 when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0 = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0
requirements.canonical: When x < 0 and `x rem |y|` < 0, `x mod y` IS `|y| + x rem |y|`.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.1 -- x rem y = x - y * (x/y) x mod y = x rem |y| when x >= 0 = 0 when x < 0 and x rem |y| = 0 = |y| + x rem |y| when x < 0 and x rem |y| < 0

requirements.canonical: For x = -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3 the value of `x mod 3` IS 0, 1, 2, 0, 1, 2, 0 respectively.
For x = -3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3 the value of `x rem 3` IS 0, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 0 respectively.

requirements.original: The predefined list operator (&) performs concatenation of values of string types, record of, set of, or array of the same root types.
requirements.canonical: The list operator `&` IS the concatenation of values of string types, record of types, set of types or arrays.

ambiguity.issue: 'array of' is used for arrays; 'string types' is not a glossary term (bitstring, hexstring, octetstring, charstring, universal charstring are meant).

requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.2 -- The predefined list operator (&) performs concatenation of values of string types, record of, set of, or array of the same root types.

requirements.original: The predefined list operator (&) performs concatenation of values of string types, record of, set of, or array of the same root types.
requirements.canonical: The operands of the list operator `&` SHALL be of the same root type.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.2 -- The predefined list operator (&) performs concatenation of values of string types, record of, set of, or array of the same root types.

requirements.original: The operation is a simple concatenation from left to right.
requirements.canonical: The list operator `&` IS a simple concatenation of its operands from left to right.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.2 -- The operation is a simple concatenation from left to right.

requirements.original: No form of arithmetic addition is implied.
requirements.canonical: The list operator `&` IS NOT any form of arithmetic addition.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.2 -- No form of arithmetic addition is implied.

requirements.original: The result type is the root type of the operands.
requirements.canonical: The result type of the list operator `&` IS the root type of its operands.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.2 -- The result type is the root type of the operands.

requirements.original: NOTE 1: In case of the list types, both the outer type (i.e. record of, set of or array) and the iterated inner type need to have the same root type in a recursive manner.
requirements.canonical: When the list operator `&` is applied to record of, set of or array values, both the outer type and the iterated inner type of the operands SHALL have the same root type, recursively.
requirements.condition: the operands are of a record of, set of or array type
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.2 -- NOTE 1: In case of the list types, both the outer type (i.e. record of, set of or array) and the iterated inner type need to have the same root type in a recursive manner.

requirements.original: NOTE 2: It is also possible to concatenate two or more value list notation expressions if the result is to be used as a record of or array of the same root type as the concatenated expressions.
requirements.canonical: Two or more value list notation expressions CAN be concatenated with `&` if the result is used as a record of or array of the same root type as the concatenated expressions.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.2 -- NOTE 2: It is also possible to concatenate two or more value list notation expressions if the result is to be used as a record of or array of the same root type as the concatenated expressions.

requirements.original: a) When the list concatenation operator is used for record of-s, set of-s and arrays, its operands shall be at least partially initialized.
requirements.canonical: When the list operator `&` is used for record of, set of or array values, its operands SHALL be at least partially initialized.
requirements.condition: the operands are record of, set of or array values
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.2 -- a) When the list concatenation operator is used for record of-s, set of-s and arrays, its operands shall be at least partially initialized.

requirements.original: The result type of all these operations is boolean.
requirements.canonical: The result type of a relational operator IS boolean.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- The result type of all these operations is boolean.

requirements.original: The relational operators less than (<), greater than (>), greater than or equal to (>=), and less than or equal to (<=) shall have only operands of type integer (including derivations of integer), float (including derivations of float), or instances of the same enumerated type.
requirements.canonical: An operand of the relational operators <, >, >= and <= SHALL be of type integer (including types derived from integer), of type float (including types derived from float), or an instance of the same enumerated type as the other operand.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- The relational operators less than (<), greater than (>), greater than or equal to (>=), and less than or equal to (<=) shall have only operands of type integer (including derivations of integer), float (including derivations of float), or instances of the same enumerated type.

requirements.original: It is not allowed to compare instances of different root types.
requirements.canonical: The operands of a relational operator SHALL NOT be instances of different root types.

ambiguity.issue: The sentence follows the rule for <, >, >=, <= but does not say whether it also covers == and !=; for == and != the next paragraph makes an exception for enumerated types. Chosen reading: it applies to <, >, >= and <=.
readings: The operands of the relational operators <, >, >= and <= SHALL NOT be instances of different root types.
The operands of any relational operator, including == and !=, SHALL NOT be instances of different root types.

requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- It is not allowed to compare instances of different root types.

requirements.original: The address type is allowed for the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators, independent of its actual type, but when its actual type differs from the types specified above, it can be compared to the literal special value null only.
requirements.canonical: A value of the address type MAY be an operand of the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators, independent of the actual type of the address type.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- The address type is allowed for the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators, independent of its actual type, but when its actual type differs from the types specified above, it can be compared to the literal special value null only.

requirements.original: The address type is allowed for the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators, independent of its actual type, but when its actual type differs from the types specified above, it can be compared to the literal special value null only.
requirements.canonical: If the actual type of the address type differs from the types for which equality is defined, a value of the address type SHALL only be compared with the special value `null`.
requirements.condition: the actual type of the address type differs from the types specified above

ambiguity.issue: "the types specified above" can mean the operand types of <, >, >=, <= (integer, float, enumerated) given in the previous paragraph, or the types for which equality rules are given in the list below. Chosen reading: the types for which equality rules exist.
readings: If the actual type of the address type is not one of the types for which equality is defined in clause 7.1.3, an address value SHALL only be compared with `null`.
If the actual type of the address type is not integer, float or an enumerated type, an address value SHALL only be compared with `null`.

requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- The address type is allowed for the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators, independent of its actual type, but when its actual type differs from the types specified above, it can be compared to the literal special value null only.

requirements.original: Operands of equality (==) and non-equality (!=) shall be completely initialized values or field references, and with the exception of enumerated types, shall be of compatible root types.
requirements.canonical: An operand of the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators SHALL be a completely initialized value or a field reference.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- Operands of equality (==) and non-equality (!=) shall be completely initialized values or field references, and with the exception of enumerated types, shall be of compatible root types.

requirements.original: Operands of equality (==) and non-equality (!=) shall be completely initialized values or field references, and with the exception of enumerated types, shall be of compatible root types.
requirements.canonical: Except for enumerated types, the operands of the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators SHALL be of compatible root types.
requirements.condition: the operands are not of enumerated types

ambiguity.issue: "compatible root types" is not a defined term; clause 6.3 defines type compatibility between types, not between root types.

requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- Operands of equality (==) and non-equality (!=) shall be completely initialized values or field references, and with the exception of enumerated types, shall be of compatible root types.

requirements.original: This implies that instances of types not mentioned below shall not be operands of equality and non-equality: The values or field references being compared shall obey the following rules.
requirements.canonical: An instance of a type for which no equality rule is given in clause 7.1.3 SHALL NOT be an operand of the equality (==) and non-equality (!=) operators.

ambiguity.issue: The list of equality rules does not mention boolean, verdicttype, objid or address types. Taken literally, these types could not be compared with == and !=, which is surely not intended. Chosen reading: the literal one, but with an open issue for the types that are not listed.
readings: Only instances of the types listed in the equality rules of clause 7.1.3 MAY be operands of == and !=; values of boolean, verdicttype or objid types SHALL NOT be compared.
Values of basic types not listed (e.g. boolean, verdicttype) MAY be compared with == and != with obvious value equality; only types without a defined equality SHALL NOT be operands.

requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- This implies that instances of types not mentioned below shall not be operands of equality and non-equality: The values or field references being compared shall obey the following rules.

requirements.original: Two field references are equal if the referenced fields are both optional fields and both fields are set to omit or if both referenced fields (regardless if they are optional or not) are initialized with values and these values are equal.
requirements.canonical: Two field references ARE equal if both referenced fields are optional fields and both are set to `omit`.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- Two field references are equal if the referenced fields are both optional fields and both fields are set to omit or if both referenced fields (regardless if they are optional or not) are initialized with values and these values are equal.

requirements.original: Two field references are equal if the referenced fields are both optional fields and both fields are set to omit or if both referenced fields (regardless if they are optional or not) are initialized with values and these values are equal.
requirements.canonical: Two field references ARE equal if both referenced fields, optional or not, are initialized with values and these values are equal.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- Two field references are equal if the referenced fields are both optional fields and both fields are set to omit or if both referenced fields (regardless if they are optional or not) are initialized with values and these values are equal.

requirements.original: A field reference is equal to a value if the referenced field is initialized with a value and both values are equal.
requirements.canonical: A field reference IS equal to a value if the referenced field is initialized with a value and both values are equal.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- A field reference is equal to a value if the referenced field is initialized with a value and both values are equal.

requirements.original: Two integer values are equal if and only if they contain the same value.
requirements.canonical: Two integer values ARE equal if and only if they contain the same value.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- Two integer values are equal if and only if they contain the same value.

requirements.original: Otherwise, normal mathematical ordering is applied. Two integer values are equal if and only if they contain the same value.
requirements.canonical: Integer values ARE ordered by the normal mathematical ordering for the relational operators <, >, >= and <=.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- Otherwise, normal mathematical ordering is applied. Two integer values are equal if and only if they contain the same value.

requirements.original: Enumerated values of the same, or different types can be compared.
requirements.canonical: Enumerated values of the same enumerated type or of different enumerated types MAY be compared.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- Enumerated values of the same, or different types can be compared.

requirements.original: In the case of different enumerated types, expression "b" of type "B" can be compared with expression "a" of type "A" if the two types "A" and "B" can be merged to a consistent larger enumerated type (i.e. where numbers are not associated with different identifiers, see also clause 6.3.2.1).
requirements.canonical: An expression of enumerated type B SHALL only be compared with an expression of a different enumerated type A if A and B can be merged into a consistent larger enumerated type, i.e. no integer value is associated with different identifiers.
requirements.condition: the operands are of different enumerated types

ambiguity.issue: In EXAMPLE 1, EDesWeekDays and EWeekDays associate the same numbers with different identifiers and therefore cannot be merged, yet the comparison v_myDesWeekDayMon == v_myWeekDayMon is shown as returning false and not as an error. Chosen reading: the normative text (comparison is not allowed).
readings: Comparing values of two enumerated types that cannot be merged SHALL cause an error.
Values of two enumerated types that cannot be merged MAY be compared, and the comparison returns false.

requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- In the case of different enumerated types, expression "b" of type "B" can be compared with expression "a" of type "A" if the two types "A" and "B" can be merged to a consistent larger enumerated type (i.e. where numbers are not associated with different identifiers, see also clause 6.3.2.1).

requirements.original: Two enumerated values are equal if and only if both their identifiers and associated integer values (associated either explicitly or implicitly, see clause 6.2.4) are the same.
requirements.canonical: Two enumerated values ARE equal if and only if both their identifiers and their associated integer values, associated explicitly or implicitly, are the same.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- Two enumerated values are equal if and only if both their identifiers and associated integer values (associated either explicitly or implicitly, see clause 6.2.4) are the same.

requirements.original: Two floating-point numbers are equal if and only if they contain the same value.
requirements.canonical: Two float values ARE equal if and only if they contain the same value.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- Two floating-point numbers are equal if and only if they contain the same value.

requirements.original: The values minus zero and plus zero are two distinct values (e.g. they are encoded differently in some standardized languages) and minus zero is less than plus zero, which represents zero.
requirements.canonical: The float values minus zero and plus zero ARE two distinct values.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- The values minus zero and plus zero are two distinct values (e.g. they are encoded differently in some standardized languages) and minus zero is less than plus zero, which represents zero.

requirements.original: The values minus zero and plus zero are two distinct values (e.g. they are encoded differently in some standardized languages) and minus zero is less than plus zero, which represents zero.
requirements.canonical: The float value minus zero IS less than plus zero, which represents zero.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- The values minus zero and plus zero are two distinct values (e.g. they are encoded differently in some standardized languages) and minus zero is less than plus zero, which represents zero.

requirements.original: Otherwise, normal mathematical ordering is applied. Two floating-point numbers are equal if and only if they contain the same value.
requirements.canonical: Float values other than the special values ARE ordered by the normal mathematical ordering.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- Otherwise, normal mathematical ordering is applied. Two floating-point numbers are equal if and only if they contain the same value.

requirements.original: The special values -infinity, `infinity and not_a_number are equal to themselves only.
requirements.canonical: Each of the special float values -infinity, infinity and not_a_number IS equal only to itself.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- The special values -infinity, `infinity and not_a_number are equal to themselves only.

requirements.original: The special` value -infinity is less than any other float value.
requirements.canonical: The special value -infinity IS less than any other float value.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- The special` value -infinity is less than any other float value.

requirements.original: The special value infinity is greater than any numerical float values and -infinity.
requirements.canonical: The special value infinity IS greater than any numerical float value and greater than -infinity.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- The special value infinity is greater than any numerical float values and -infinity.

requirements.original: The special value not_a_number is greater than any other float value (including infinity).
requirements.canonical: The special value not_a_number IS greater than any other float value, including infinity.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- The special value not_a_number is greater than any other float value (including infinity).

requirements.original: Two charstring or two universal charstring values are equal if and only if they have equal lengths and the characters at all positions are the same.
requirements.canonical: Two charstring values, or two universal charstring values, ARE equal if and only if they have equal lengths and the characters at all positions are the same.
requirements.header: // @requirement: 7.1.3 -- Two charstring or two universal charstring values are equal if and only if they have equal lengths and the characters at all positions are the same.
